A8Why an adaptive state model needs another changing state

An input steps up and stays up, and the output returns exactly to its old value. Where did the input go? One line of bookkeeping answers it for a stated kind of system: some other state has changed, and it holds the input. In Lecture 9's high-gain loop the only slow state is the output, so the output itself holds the input, as an error.

The questionA step in, a pulse out

Perfect adaptation is a transient response followed by return to the same steady output. Hold an input until the system rests, step it to a new value, and hold it there. The output can rise or fall before returning. Figure 21 shows a rise. Chemotaxis in A12 will show a fall. A nonzero final offset is the adaptation error. We call adaptation near-perfect only after stating a tolerance.

Two different robustness questions

Input invariance keeps the steady output independent of the input at fixed parameters. A parameter change may preserve input invariance while moving the value to which the output returns.

A fixed set point survives a specified change of the system. State which parameters change and which reference parameters stay fixed. Chemotaxis in A12 separates these two questions. The load comparison in A16 turns the distinction into an experiment.

The bookkeepingSome other state must change

One line of bookkeeping says where the input went, for a stated kind of system. Take a model s˙=f(s,u)\dot s=f(s,u), where s collects the model's states and u is its input. Suppose it rests at a finite steady state before the step, the input is then held at its new value, and the model settles to a finite steady state after it. Suppose also that the output is read from the state and responds to the step, so the step changes the vector field f at the old rest. Then the old rest is no longer a rest under the new input, and the new steady state differs from the old one. The output is the same at both, so the difference sits in some other state. That state holds the input, and we call it the memory.

The argument has a domain, and three cases lie outside it. It does not cover an output that feeds through the input directly, a pulse driven by the input's rate of change, or hidden variables that never settle. So it is not a theorem about every observed pulse. It is a statement about models that settle, with the output read from their state.

Lecture 9's loopThe output itself holds the input, as an error

In Lecture 9's high-gain loop the output itself holds the input. A repressor represses its own gene, and growth dilutes it. Promoter binding is fast, so the repressor total is the loop's only slow state, and it is the output. A change in production or removal moves the balance of the two, and a production curve of finite slope cannot rebalance at the same output (Figure 22). So the steady state must move, and the only state that can move is the output. It holds the input, as an error.

The size of that error is Black's factor. Write the repressed production as f(x)f(x), with x the output, and let the loop gain be H=−dln⁡f/dln⁡xH=-d\ln f/d\ln x at the set point. H is positive, because production falls as the output rises. In that model a small relative change in removal moves the set point by about 1/(1+H)1/(1+H) of it. That factor is a sensitivity to small changes. Figure 22 shows a finite, fourfold change, solved exactly, so its shifts are not given by the factor. The error is small when the loop gain is high, but never zero, because a finite slope always leaves the two crossings apart. Removing it needs a separate state that can hold the input while the output returns.

Find where a persistent input is held: in a model that settles, with the output read from its state and responding to the step, some other state must change. If the output is the only slow state, expect it to hold the input as an error, about 1/(1+H)1/(1+H) of a small relative change in a high-gain loop, and never zero.

A9Compare an integral loop with a linear subtractive compensator

Give the memory its own state, and let it change at a rate equal to the error. Then it can rest only where the error is zero, whatever the plant's constants, and at rest it holds the action that cancels the input. Whether the loop comes to rest is a separate test. The obvious alternative, a compensator that subtracts a measured copy of the input, stores nothing and needs a matched constant.

The constructionA state that changes at the rate of the error

An integral state changes at a rate equal to the error, so it can rest only where the error is zero. Take the simplest plant: an output x measured from its set point, so that x is the error, pushed by a constant disturbance d and relaxing at unit rate. Add a memory z that changes at the rate x and acts back on the output with gain kIk_I (Figure 2):

x˙=−x+d−kIz,z˙=x.\dot x=-x+d-k_I z,\qquad \dot z=x.(E1)

Here d is the input, kIk_I is the integral gain, and time is in units of the plant's relaxation time. The second equation lets z stop changing only where x=0x=0. That holds whatever the plant's constants are, because the plant does not appear in it. Both x and z are signed coordinates, not concentrations.

The memoryAt rest it holds the compensating action

At rest the memory holds the action that cancels the input, not the input itself. Setting both rates of (E1) to zero gives x=0x=0 and z∗=d/kIz^*=d/k_I. The memory stores d divided by the gain through which it acts, in the controller's units: exactly the action kIz∗=dk_Iz^*=d that cancels the input. The plant's constants do not enter. Give the output a relaxation rate γ\gamma in place of 1, and across six pairs of γ\gamma and kIk_I the loop still rests at x=0x=0, each time with z∗=d/kIz^*=d/k_I (model calculation).

The error is signed, and the output overshoots before it returns. After a unit step at kI=2k_I=2, the output rises to 0.448, swings below its set point to −0.137-0.137 at 3.29 time units after the step, then returns, while z climbs past d/kId/k_I and settles there (Figure 23, left, model predictions). The swing below zero is real: x is a deviation, so a negative value only means the output sits below its set point.

Whether the loop rests at all is a separate test. The integral fixes where a rest can be, not whether the loop reaches it. Remove the plant's own relaxation, the term −x-x, and the same memory makes the loop oscillate for ever around the rest, with amplitude 0.707 and period 4.44 (Figure 23, right, model predictions). The rest exists and has zero error, but the loop never reaches it. With the relaxation present, both eigenvalues of (E1) have negative real parts whenever the relaxation rate and kIk_I are positive, so the rest is stable.

The alternativeA subtractive compensator stores nothing

Subtracting a measured copy of the input is another route, and it needs a matched constant. Take the plant x˙=−ax+u+d\dot x=-ax+u+d, with relaxation rate a, and let a compensator measure d and act at once with u=−c du=-c\,d, where c is its scaling constant. The output settles at an offset (1−c) d/a(1-c)\,d/a, which is zero only at c=1c=1 (Figure 24, left). The compensator acts on a measurement and stores nothing, so it needs the input measured and scaled to match the plant. If the plant's input gain changes after the compensator was set, the offset returns, while the integral loop still rests at zero error (Figure 24, right, model calculation).

When matched, the compensator never lets the output move, so A8's bookkeeping has nothing to explain. The output does not respond to the step, so this compensator lies outside the domain of A8. The claim is about this compensator, not about feedforward adaptation in general. A15 shows an incoherent feedforward loop that needs no matched constant.

Build a memory that removes a steady error: let a state change at the rate of the error, so that it can rest only at zero error, holding the compensating action z∗=d/kIz^*=d/k_I. Then test stability separately. Recognize a subtractive compensator by its matched constant: its offset is (1−c) d/a(1-c)\,d/a.

A10Compare internal model theorems with different hypotheses

The main internal model statement gives the classical linear setting. Other hypotheses support different necessity theorems.

Other theoremsHypotheses decide what a theorem proves

Other theorems reach an internal model from different hypotheses. Sontag's 2003 theorem assumes that the system adapts to a class of signals, together with a signal-detection condition and bounded trajectories. It assumes no split into plant and controller, and no robustness requirement.2 It concludes that the system contains a subsystem that can generate those signals. So the principle is a family of theorems that answer different questions (optional A1).

An adapting trace alone does not prove that an integrator is present. A trace shows the output returning. Each theorem also needs its hypotheses checked: what the controller sees, which disturbances act, which changes of the plant are allowed, and whether the loop is stable. The table sets the two theorems side by side.

Francis and Wonham (1976)Sontag (2003)
SettingLinear, time-invariant systems, extended only locally to weakly nonlinear plants with constant signalsNonlinear systems that meet the theorem's technical assumptions
Structure assumedA plant and a controller that sees only the errorNo split into plant and controller
SignalsDisturbances from a known class, constants hereA class of external signals, constants here
Other hypothesesA stable closed loop, and regulation that survives small changes of the plantAdaptation itself, bounded trajectories and signal detection
ConclusionThe controller contains a copy of the signal generator: for constants, a mode at zero frequencyThe system contains a subsystem that generates the signals

State the internal model principle with its hypotheses: for constant disturbances, a controller that sees only the error, keeps the loop stable and regulates under small changes of the plant must contain a mode at zero frequency, an integral of the error, which need not be one molecule. Before concluding that an adapting circuit integrates, check which theorem's hypotheses it meets.

A11Revisit the three chemical constructions

The main comparison restores the signed-charge diagram and all three chemical routes. The saturated-removal example, antithetic difference and multiplicative-growth calculation develop their conditions separately.

A12Audit chemotaxis parameter changes and finite modification capacity

Escherichia coli adapts to attractant: after a step, its tumbling returns to its old rate while the attractant stays. The memory is receptor methylation. In Barkai and Leibler's reduced module, methylation can rest only at one receptor activity, whatever the attractant, so it integrates the activity's error. More generally, a saturated modification cycle integrates the imbalance of its two fluxes, feedback from the output makes that an error integral, and the cycle's total bounds the range.

The pathwayAttractant, kinase, tumble, and two methylation enzymes

In E. coli, attractant slows a receptor-coupled kinase, and the cell tumbles less. Attractant binds the receptor. The receptor-coupled kinase CheA slows, so less of the response regulator CheY is phosphorylated, and phosphorylated CheY is what makes the motor tumble (Figure 7, left). So a step up in attractant lowers the tumbling rate. Then the tumbling returns to its old rate while the attractant stays.

The memory is receptor methylation, set by two enzymes. CheR adds methyl groups to the receptor and CheB removes them.4 Methylation raises the receptor's activity, and attractant lowers it. In the cell, CheA also activates CheB by phosphorylating it, a regulation that Yi and colleagues keep apart from the model they analyze.5

The modelMethylation rests only at one activity

Keep the pathway and its model apart. Barkai and Leibler's model does not treat CheB's phosphorylation by CheA explicitly.6 Their reduced module has CheR working at saturation, at a constant rate, and CheB acting only on active receptors, at a rate set by the activity alone (their eq. (E1), printed p. 916, written for EmE_m, the amount of modified receptor). Our teaching model adopts that activity-only rate form, scaled for the mean methylation per receptor:

m˙=VR−VB aKB+a,\dot m=V_R-V_B\,\frac{a}{K_B+a},(E2)

where m is the mean methylation per receptor, a is the receptor activity, VRV_R is the rate at which CheR methylates, VBV_B is CheB's maximal demethylation rate, and KBK_B is the activity at which CheB works at half that rate. CheR works at a constant rate, and CheB's rate depends on the activity alone.

So methylation can rest only at one activity, whatever the attractant and whatever the methylation. Setting m˙=0\dot m=0 in (E2) gives

a∗=KBVRVB−VR.a^*=\frac{K_B V_R}{V_B-V_R}.(E3)

Activity is a fraction between 0 and 1 here, so this rest must be an activity the receptors can reach. It needs 0<a∗<10<a^*<1, which holds when VB>(1+KB)VRV_B>(1+K_B)V_R, not only when VR<VBV_R<V_B. It also needs a methylation level between zero and the number of sites that gives a=a∗a=a^*. Methylation therefore integrates a function of the activity's error.

The key property is independence from m and attractant at fixed activity, not saturation of both enzymes. The demethylation term still depends on a. What matters is that it depends on nothing else, so the rate of change of m vanishes at one activity only.

A more careful model and a teaching law are different objects. Yi, Huang, Simon and Doyle give a more careful weighted methylation coordinate under four stated assumptions.5 A linear law m˙=r1−r2a\dot m=r_1-r_2a, with positive constants r1r_1 and r2r_2, may serve as a teaching model, declared as such.

Model details, outside the clock

Three chemotaxis models appear in this section, and they stay distinct. The pathway of Figure 7, left, is the biology, in which CheA also phosphorylates CheB. The teaching model (E2) adopts the activity-only form of Barkai and Leibler's reduced module, with CheB's rate set by the activity alone (Figure 8). The bounded model of Figures 9 and 31 is (E2) with limits on the sites added.

In the teaching model the activity is the fast equilibrium of a cluster of N receptors. With mean methylation m and attractant L,

a(m,L)=11+eF,a(m,L)=\frac{1}{1+e^{F}},
F=N[ϵ0−ϵ1m+ln⁡1+L/KI1+L/KA],F=N\Big[\epsilon_0-\epsilon_1m+\ln\frac{1+L/K_I}{1+L/K_A}\Big],

where KIK_I and KAK_A are the attractant's dissociation constants for an inactive and an active receptor, and ϵ0\epsilon_0 and ϵ1\epsilon_1 set the activity's offset and its rise per methyl group. The illustrative constants are N=6N=6, ϵ0=ϵ1=1\epsilon_0=\epsilon_1=1, KI=1K_I=1, KA=100K_A=100, M=4M=4, VR=1V_R=1, VB=2V_B=2 and KB=1/3K_B=1/3, so (E3) gives a∗=1/3a^*=1/3.

The bounded model multiplies each enzyme's rate by a site factor. CheR's rate carries sR=(M−m)/(κR+M−m)s_R=(M-m)/(\kappa_R+M-m) and CheB's carries sB=m/(κB+m)s_B=m/(\kappa_B+m), with κR=κB=10−4\kappa_R=\kappa_B=10^{-4}, so each factor is close to 1 inside the range and vanishes at its end. In all three runs L is in units of KIK_I, m in methyl groups per receptor, and time in the time CheR takes to add one methyl group per receptor at its baseline rate VRV_R.

The mechanism or curve is shown in the main-route figure. The calculation below supplies its detailed audit.

The behaviorMethylation climbs and holds, and the activity returns exactly

After an attractant step, the activity drops at once and returns exactly, while methylation climbs and holds (Figure 8). In the reduced model the activity is the receptor's fast equilibrium, a function of methylation and attractant, so it drops at the instant of the step. Methylation then climbs from 0.88 to 2.63 methyl groups per receptor and holds there, and the activity returns to a∗=1/3a^*=1/3, with an error below 10−910^{-9} (model predictions). The attractant is stored in methylation.

A8's bookkeeping applies to the fuller model, where the activity is a fast state. The reduced model writes the activity as an algebraic function a(m,L)a(m,L), which responds to the attractant directly. That is the case A8 excludes, an output that feeds through the input. In the fuller model the receptor's activity is a fast state of its own, and the argument applies there. The memory is still methylation.

Changing CheR can preserve input invariance while moving the set point. Cut CheR tenfold and the adapted activity (E3) falls from 1/3 to 0.0175. The half-time of the return grows from 1.85 to 17.5 time units. The activity still returns to its own new a∗a^* because that value remains reachable within the methylation range (Figure 8, right, model predictions). Neither the reference activity nor the recovery time is invariant to this change.

Model meets measurement

Alon, Surette, Barkai and Leibler varied the levels of the chemotaxis proteins in E. coli. The steady-state behavior and the adaptation time varied strongly with them, while the precision of adaptation stayed robust (p. 168). As CheR varied between about 0.4 and 6 times its wild-type level, the adaptation time changed more than 20-fold, from 23 ± 2 min to about 1 min, and the steady tumbling frequency about threefold, while adaptation stayed precise within experimental error. Wild-type cells adapted with a measured precision of 0.98 ± 0.05 (p. 169).4 That is the pattern of Figure 8: the reference value and the timing move, and the precision does not.

The input, activity and methylation response is shown in the main-route figure. The surrounding calculation supplies its detailed parameter audit.

GeneralizeA saturated cycle integrates, and feedback makes it an error integral

An open modification cycle whose two enzymes are saturated integrates the imbalance of their fluxes. Take a protein Y that an enzyme E modifies to YPY_P and an enzyme F demodifies. While both enzymes are saturated, their fluxes are nearly kEqEk_Eq_E and kFqFk_Fq_F, whatever the amounts of Y and YPY_P, where kEk_E and kFk_F are their catalytic rate constants and qEq_E and qFq_F their totals. Then q˙YP≈kEqE−kFqF\dot q_{Y_P}\approx k_Eq_E-k_Fq_F inside the cycle's interior. The modified total runs toward one end of the cycle whenever the two capacities differ, which is why the open cycle has a steep static response, zero-order ultrasensitivity (Figure 25, left). Goldbeter and Koshland showed that the switch is far more abrupt when both converting enzymes are saturated, and traced it to two enzymes acting in opposite directions on a target protein whose total is conserved (p. 6841).7 Their analysis concerns this static switch, not integration.

The cycle becomes an error integrator only when the sensed output sets that imbalance by feedback. Let an output a, read from YPY_P, set F's rate through an increasing function g(a)g(a), and let a held disturbance u act on the output too, a=a(qYP,u)a=a(q_{Y_P},u), as attractant acts on receptor activity. The cycle then obeys q˙YP≈kEqE−kFqF g(a)\dot q_{Y_P}\approx k_Eq_E-k_Fq_F\,g(a), so it can rest only where g(a)=kEqE/(kFqF)g(a)=k_Eq_E/(k_Fq_F) (Figure 25, right). The fixed capacities set that rest a∗a^*, whatever u, and the memory qYPq_{Y_P} shifts with u to hold the output there. Receptor activity sets demethylation in exactly this way. A switch alone does not adapt. In Ma and colleagues' search over three-node enzyme circuits, the feedback design adapted by this zero-order ultrasensitivity, which needs the two enzymes of the buffering node to work at saturation.8

The loop rejects the disturbance, not a change in its own capacities. A change in qEq_E or qFq_F moves the set point itself, and the loop does not reject it. Cutting CheR moved a∗a^* in exactly this way in Figure 8.

The rangeThe memory is bounded by the cycle's total

The memory is bounded by the cycle's total, so the range is bounded too. A receptor offers a finite number of methylation sites, and methylation cannot exceed it. Once the attractant asks for more methylation than the sites allow, the zero-order law fails at the boundary and adaptation ends. In a bounded version of the model, in which methylation slows as the sites fill, the law (E2) alone would need more than its M=4M=4 sites beyond L=27.8 KIL=27.8\,K_I. The steady activity stays within 5% of a∗a^* only up to L=28.1 KIL=28.1\,K_I, and at L=100 KIL=100\,K_I it settles 98.8% below it (Figure 9, model predictions with a declared teaching construction).

The site count and the measured range are measurements, not model outputs. The model's four sites are an illustrative choice. The aspartate receptor Tar has four methylation sites (p. 123).9 Neumann and colleagues measured where the range ends. In E. coli, adaptation grew increasingly imprecise at higher attractant concentrations, and for the attractant MeAsp the adapted kinase activity fell to about 70% of its prestimulus level by 10 mM, a value read from their Figure 21B. They attribute the imprecision to a gradual saturation of the methylation sites, which is their inference from the data, not a direct measurement (pp. 1–3).10

The mechanism or curve is shown in the main-route figure. The calculation below supplies its detailed audit.

Read chemotaxis as an integral loop: methylation is the memory, it rests only at the activity a∗=KBVR/(VB−VR)a^*=K_BV_R/(V_B-V_R), which must lie between 0 and 1, and its range ends when the sites fill. Recognize a zero-order integrator in any saturated modification cycle whose reverse flux is set by its own output.

A13Distinguish the adapting pools in the two-cycle mechanism

Can two modification cycles, written with every complex, build the zero-order integrator of A12? Approximated enzyme by enzyme, their conditions contradict each other. Lecture 8's method writes the totals, chooses one joint regime, and finds that the design adapts there. The exact flux balance constrains one complex at rest. A measured pool follows that complex when the other forms in the pool are small.

The designTwo modification cycles close a feedback loop

The design is a two-node feedback loop, written with every complex. It is the reduction that Jeynes-Smith and Araujo discuss of Ma and colleagues' search over three-node circuits, not a design printed in Ma et al.11 An input I modifies a protein A to A∗A^*. The modified A∗A^* modifies a protein B to B∗B^*. The modified B∗B^* demodifies A∗A^*, and a fixed enzyme E demodifies B∗B^*. Four complexes carry these steps, numbered as Jeynes-Smith and Araujo number them: C1C_1 is I bound to A, C2C_2 is A∗A^* bound to B∗B^*, C3C_3 is B bound to A∗A^*, and C4C_4 is B∗B^* bound to E (Figure 12). It is problem set 3, problem 2 (2025).

Notation, as in every lecture

A bare symbol such as A∗A^* is a free concentration. A total such as qA∗=A∗+C2+C3q_{A^*}=A^*+C_2+C_3 counts a form over every state that contains it. Here the complexes keep the paper's numbers, C1C_1 to C4C_4, and each is named by its constituents in the text. Each binding has a constant K. At binding equilibrium K is a dissociation constant: KA1C1=IAK_{A1}C_1=IA, KA2C2=A∗B∗K_{A2}C_2=A^*B^*, KB1C3=A∗BK_{B1}C_3=A^*B and KB2C4=B∗EK_{B2}C_4=B^*E. A model that resolves every binding and catalytic step satisfies the same relations only at its steady state, and with Michaelis constants, K=(k−+kcat)/k+K=(k_-+k_\mathrm{cat})/k_+, which approach the dissociation constants when catalysis is much slower than unbinding.

Each catalytic step changes one modified total, and the balances follow. Binding is fast and at equilibrium, as in Lecture 8's model class, and catalysis is slow. The modified totals qA∗=A∗+C2+C3q_{A^*}=A^*+C_2+C_3 and qB∗=B∗+C2+C4q_{B^*}=B^*+C_2+C_4 change only by catalysis,

q˙A∗=kA1C1−kA2C2,q˙B∗=kB1C3−kB2C4,\dot q_{A^*}=k_{A1}C_1-k_{A2}C_2,\qquad \dot q_{B^*}=k_{B1}C_3-k_{B2}C_4,(E4)

where kA1k_{A1} and kA2k_{A2} are the catalytic rate constants of the A cycle, and kB1k_{B1} and kB2k_{B2} those of the B cycle.

The mechanism or curve is shown in the main-route figure. The calculation below supplies its detailed audit.

The collisionTwo approximations, one binding

Approximate each enzyme separately by Michaelis-Menten, and two inequalities on the same binding collide. The A cycle's usual approximation counts every modified A as free A∗A^*, available to B∗B^*, which needs B's total far below KB1K_{B1}, so that little A∗A^* is bound to B. The B cycle's zero order, with A∗A^* saturated by B, needs B's total far above KB1K_{B1} (Figure 26, top). Both conditions concern the one binding of A∗A^* and B in C3C_3, so they cannot hold together. This does not make Michaelis-Menten kinetics inconsistent in general. It shows that these two approximations cannot hold together here.

The joint regimeLecture 8's method finds the design

Lecture 8's method finds the design instead: write the six totals and choose one winner for each. The totals are those of I, of the unmodified A and B, of the modified A∗A^* and B∗B^*, and of E. Keep the choice that makes the B cycle zero order: I, A and B free, C3C_3 carrying the modified A, C2C_2 carrying B∗B^*, and C4C_4 carrying E. In that joint regime, at leading order, the balances (E4) become

q˙A∗≈kA1qIKA1 qA−kA2 qB∗,q˙B∗≈kB1 qA∗−kB2 qE,\begin{aligned}\dot q_{A^*}&\approx k_{A1}\frac{q_I}{K_{A1}}\,q_A-k_{A2}\,q_{B^*},\\ \dot q_{B^*}&\approx k_{B1}\,q_{A^*}-k_{B2}\,q_E,\end{aligned}(E5)

where qA=A+C1q_A=A+C_1 is the unmodified-A total and qIq_I the input total.

In that regime the modified-B total integrates the error, and the rest is stable. The second balance of (E5) changes at the rate kB1(qA∗−σ)k_{B1}(q_{A^*}-\sigma), with

σ=kB2kB1 qE,\sigma=\frac{k_{B2}}{k_{B1}}\,q_E,(E6)

so it can rest only where the modified-A total equals σ\sigma, whatever the input: the modified-B total integrates the error. Jeynes-Smith and Araujo derive the same set point in the limit of saturated B-cycle enzymes.11 Catalysis conserves the A-protein inventory A0=qA+qA∗A_0=q_A+q_{A^*}. At the proposed rest, the unmodified pool is therefore qA=A0−σq_A=A_0-\sigma. A positive rest needs A0>σA_0>\sigma. The B-protein inventory B0=qB+qB∗B_0=q_B+q_{B^*} must also hold the B in C3C_3 and in the memory, so the leading approximation needs B0>σ+qB∗B_0>\sigma+q_{B^*}.

Conservation also supplies the damping. Substitute qA=A0−qA∗q_A=A_0-q_{A^*} into (E5). Increasing the modified pool then leaves less unmodified A for the input to modify. The resulting linearization has a negative trace and a positive determinant, so the feasible rest of this leading model is stable (Figure 26, bottom). This is a local result inside the joint regime. The exposition derives the inventory bounds, and its stability calculation keeps the conservation law explicit. Optional A7 audits the winner conditions.

The joint regime holds over an interval of inputs, and there it justifies the leading-order model. At the illustrative parameter set PT, whose constants optional A7 lists, every winner holds by 5:1 or better for input totals from qI=0.052q_I=0.052 to 20 (a model prediction). Inside that interval the balances (E5) are a valid leading order. How far each measured quantity adapts is a separate question, which the exact model answers next.

The observableFlux balance picks what adapts

Then ask which measured quantity adapts, and let the exact identity answer. The modified-B total changes at kB1C3−kB2C4k_{B1}C_3-k_{B2}C_4, exactly, by (E4). At rest C3=(kB2/kB1)C4C_3=(k_{B2}/k_{B1})C_4, and since C4=qE−EC_4=q_E-E, this is C3=σ(1−E/qE)C_3=\sigma(1-E/q_E) exactly, with E the free enzyme. In this regime C4C_4 holds nearly all of qEq_E, so flux balance pins the complex C3C_3 near σ\sigma.

The partial pool follows C3C_3 when its free contribution is small. Define the partial pool as A∗+C3A^*+C_3. It excludes C2C_2, the other complex containing modified A. Jeynes-Smith and Araujo identify this partial pool as the observable that tracks their set point within a tolerance and input range (p. 5).11 At set PT it stays within 5% of σ\sigma from qI=0.065q_I=0.065 to at least 10410^4, the end of the computed grid. The errors are −0.93%, −0.01%, +0.26% and +0.35% at qI=0.3q_I=0.3, 1, 3 and 9 (Figure 27, model predictions). Its exact error is −E/qE+A∗/σ-E/q_E+A^*/\sigma (optional A7). At low input E leaves saturation, the negative term grows, and the tracking range ends.

The memory sits in another complex, so the full total drifts with the input. The memory, the modified-B total, sits mostly in C2C_2, a complex with A∗A^*. So the full modified-A total A∗+C2+C3A^*+C_2+C_3 exceeds the partial pool by exactly C2C_2, which carries the memory and grows with the input. The full total adapts only while the memory stays small next to σ\sigma. At set PT, C2C_2 is 0.0097σ0.0097\sigma at qI=1q_I=1 and 0.082σ0.082\sigma at qI=10q_I=10, and the full total stays within 5% of σ\sigma only from qI=0.064q_I=0.064 to 5.23, with errors of −0.63%, +0.96%, +3.1% and +7.9% at qI=0.3q_I=0.3, 1, 3 and 9 (Figure 27, model predictions).

Free A∗A^* is a third quantity, and it fails in a different way. Binding equilibrium gives free A∗=KB1C3/BA^*=K_{B1}C_3/B exactly, and a resolved model gives the same at its steady state with the Michaelis constant. So free A∗A^* holds only as well as free B does. At set PT free B stays far larger than the complexes that draw on it, so free A∗A^* varies by at most 5% from qI=0.1q_I=0.1 to 10410^4. Yet it sits near 0.0041σ0.0041\sigma, 99.6% below σ\sigma (Figure 27, model predictions). It is nearly constant at a value far below σ\sigma, so not tracking σ\sigma and not being input invariant are different failures.

Check a proposed enzymatic integrator with Lecture 8's method: write the totals, choose one joint regime, and verify the integral there. Then find the adapting observable from the exact flux balance, the pool dominated by the pinned complex, read its range from the exact model rather than from the regime's edges, and expect a total that also counts the memory's complex to drift with the input.

A14Calculate antithetic dilution, windup and stability limits

Two controllers that sequester each other one to one store the error as the difference of their totals. The identity is exact at every binding allocation, so any rest has X=μ/θX=\mu/\theta, whatever the plant, and the actuator's level is the compensating action. The identity does not guarantee three things: a reachable set point, exactness under dilution, and a loop that settles.

The identityThe difference of two totals integrates the error

Recall Lecture 9's sequestering pair. A reference makes the actuator Z1Z_1 at rate μ\mu. The output X makes the sensor Z2Z_2 at rate θX\theta X. The actuator makes X at rate kZ1kZ_1, and X is removed at rate γX\gamma X. The two controllers bind each other reversibly into CZ1Z2C_{Z_1Z_2}, which is removed at frequency δC\delta_C (Figure 15). With the controller totals qZ1=Z1+CZ1Z2q_{Z_1}=Z_1+C_{Z_1Z_2} and qZ2=Z2+CZ1Z2q_{Z_2}=Z_2+C_{Z_1Z_2},

ddt(qZ1−qZ2)=μ−θX,\frac{d}{dt}\big(q_{Z_1}-q_{Z_2}\big)=\mu-\theta X,(E7)

because binding, unbinding and removal of the pair change both totals equally (Lecture 9, §6).

The identity (E7) is exact at every binding allocation. It needs no dominant complex, no fast binding and no zero-order limit. Any rest therefore has X=μ/θX=\mu/\theta, whatever the plant.

The difference stores the error, and the actuator holds the compensating action. The difference of the controller totals is the integral of the error. At rest the actuator's level is the compensating action, moved to whatever value the plant needs. In the plant drawn here, kZ1∗=γX∗kZ_1^*=\gamma X^*, so Z1∗=γμ/(kθ)Z_1^*=\gamma\mu/(k\theta). A faster removal of X, the disturbance, is met by a higher actuator level, while X returns to μ/θ\mu/\theta. In the model, when the removal rate of X doubles, X dips to 0.6297 at 1.007 time units after the step and returns, staying within 1% of μ/θ\mu/\theta from 6.474 after the step. The actuator Z1Z_1 moves from 1 to 2, and the error integral qZ1−qZ2q_{Z_1}-q_{Z_2} from 0.98 to 1.99 (Figure 16, top left, model predictions in units of μ/θ\mu/\theta and 1/γref1/\gamma_\mathrm{ref}).

The mechanism or curve is shown in the main-route figure. The calculation below supplies its detailed audit.

The limitsWhat the identity does not guarantee

The identity does not guarantee three things, and the first two are reachability and exactness under dilution. The set point must be reachable. If the plant cannot make enough output, X stays below μ/θ\mu/\theta, the difference keeps growing, and a controller pool accumulates without bound: windup. The controllers must also not be diluted. Growth dilutes free and bound controllers alike, the complex cancels from the difference, and the free controllers leave a leak, −λ(Z1−Z2)-\lambda(Z_1-Z_2), on the right side of (E7). That leak in general breaks exactness. Adaptation is then near-perfect only when the leak is small enough, so growth by itself does not guarantee a small error.

Worked windup calculation (optional reading)

In the model, an unreachable set point winds the controller up. Give the actuation a ceiling, kZ1/(1+Z1/Ksat)kZ_1/(1+Z_1/K_\mathrm{sat}) with k=1k=1 and Ksat=2K_\mathrm{sat}=2, and triple the removal of X for 100 time units. The output can then reach at most Xcap=kKsat/(3γref)=2/3X_\mathrm{cap}=kK_\mathrm{sat}/(3\gamma_\mathrm{ref})=2/3, below μ/θ=1\mu/\theta=1. X starts above that ceiling and, after an initial transient, stays below it, at most 0.6366. Throughout, it obeys the comparison bound X(t)≤Xcap+(X(t0)−Xcap)e−r(t−t0)X(t)\le X_\mathrm{cap}+(X(t_0)-X_\mathrm{cap})e^{-r(t-t_0)}, where r is the total first-order removal rate in force. So the error integral has a lower bound that grows at μ−θXcap=1/3\mu-\theta X_\mathrm{cap}=1/3 per unit time, and qZ1q_{Z_1} grows without bound for as long as the set point stays out of reach, a statement about long times. In the finite run it reaches 43.13 by the release, climbing at 0.372 per unit time near the end. After release X overshoots to 1.9 and takes 65.46 time units to return within 1% (Figure 16, top right, model predictions).

Under growth, the leak leaves a steady error. Dilute every species at rate λ\lambda, and the signed relative error of X at rest is (X∗−μ/θ)/(μ/θ)=−λ(Z1∗−Z2∗)/μ(X^*-\mu/\theta)/(\mu/\theta)=-\lambda(Z_1^*-Z_2^*)/\mu. Its sign is opposite to that of Z1∗−Z2∗Z_1^*-Z_2^*, so the rest can sit on either side of μ/θ\mu/\theta. With the model's constants Z1∗Z_1^* exceeds Z2∗Z_2^*, so the rest falls below μ/θ\mu/\theta, and the steady error grows with the dilution rate: −0.98%, −4.9%, −9.8%, −19% and −43% at λ=0.01\lambda=0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5, in units of γref\gamma_\mathrm{ref} (Figure 16, bottom, model predictions). The rest is then no longer protected from the plant: at λ=0.1\lambda=0.1, a doubling of the removal of X moves X from 0.9025 to 0.8272.

Near-perfect needs a stated tolerance, and this page uses 5%. At the model's constants the steady error stays within 5% at λ=0.05γref\lambda=0.05\gamma_\mathrm{ref} and not at 0.1γref0.1\gamma_\mathrm{ref}. In general the size of the relative error is λ∣Z1∗−Z2∗∣/μ\lambda|Z_1^*-Z_2^*|/\mu, so it is small when the controllers turn over fast against growth. Qian and Del Vecchio prove this: if the controller's reactions are all much faster than dilution, the error from leaky integration becomes negligible (p. 1).12

The mechanism or curve is shown in the main-route figure. The calculation below supplies its detailed audit.

The third guarantee that is missing is stability, and it depends on the plant. With the linear one-stage plant drawn here, reversible sequestration and no controller leak, the rest is locally stable for every choice of positive constants (the stability audit below gives the certificate). That is a property of this plant, not of every one-stage plant. With a two-stage plant, in which Z1Z_1 drives an mRNA that makes X, a high actuation gain can make the rest unstable. Instability is not yet an oscillation: a sustained cycle is shown by simulation, not inferred from an eigenvalue. Briat, Gupta and Khammash note that the deterministic controller oscillates in an instability region, where its stochastic counterpart still adapts in the mean (p. 24, optional A4).13

The mRNA stage adds a lag, and a loop with a lag can overcorrect. A change of the actuator now reaches X only after the mRNA has changed. Meanwhile the controllers keep integrating the error, so when X finally responds the actuator has already moved too far, and the output overshoots the other way. This argument shows only that instability is possible. Whether it occurs, and at which gains, needs the test, and here it is not monotone in gain: each unstable window below closes again at higher gain.

The two-stage results use the annihilation controller, the form Briat, Gupta and Khammash analyze. In it, one Z1Z_1 and one Z2Z_2 remove each other in a single composite step, Z1+Z2⇝∅Z_1+Z_2\rightsquigarrow\varnothing, with the rate law ηZ1Z2\eta Z_1Z_2, where η\eta is the annihilation rate constant: Z˙1=μ−ηZ1Z2\dot Z_1=\mu-\eta Z_1Z_2 and Z˙2=θX−ηZ1Z2\dot Z_2=\theta X-\eta Z_1Z_2. The two-stage plant adds an mRNA M, with M˙=kZ1−γMM\dot M=kZ_1-\gamma_MM and X˙=βM−γXX\dot X=\beta M-\gamma_XX.

Numerical stability window and periodic orbit (optional reading)

With the annihilation controller, high gain destabilizes the rest only inside a window. At η=100\eta=100 and μ=θ=β=γM=γX=1\mu=\theta=\beta=\gamma_M=\gamma_X=1, the rest is unstable only for actuation gains between k=2.0038k=2.0038 and 49.904, and it is stable again above 49.904 (Figure 28, left, model predictions). At each edge of the window the rest's slowest mode, an oscillation, switches between decaying and growing. With reversible binding in place of annihilation, the window is 2.0752 to 24.094, so each mechanism has its own window.

Inside the window, a simulation shows a sustained cycle. At k=10k=10 the rest's slowest mode grows at the rate 0.2478. Started 1% off the rest, the loop with the annihilation controller settles onto a periodic orbit of period 8.047, on which X swings between 0.141 and 2.577 while its average over a cycle stays at μ/θ\mu/\theta. The error integral requires that average, because the difference Z1−Z2Z_1-Z_2 returns to its start after each period. Nearby trajectories return to the cycle (stability audit below). Below the window, at k=1k=1, X returns to μ/θ\mu/\theta after the removal of X doubles (Figure 28, right, model predictions).

Stability audit (optional reading)

Three checks back the stability statements of this section. The first is symbolic, and the other two are numerical. Each is a standard test, stated here with what it found.

The one-stage rest passes the Routh-Hurwitz test for every positive constant. Its linearization has the quartic characteristic polynomial p(s)=a4s4+a3s3+a2s2+a1s+a0p(s)=a_4s^4+a_3s^3+a_2s^2+a_1s+a_0, and every coefficient is a sum of positive terms. For such a quartic the remaining Routh-Hurwitz condition is a3a2a1−a4a12−a32a0>0a_3a_2a_1-a_4a_1^2-a_3^2a_0>0. Over a positive denominator, that expression has a numerator of 65 positive terms, so the rest is locally stable whatever the positive constants. With annihilation in place of reversible binding the polynomial is a cubic, s3+c2s2+c1s+c0s^3+c_2s^2+c_1s+c_0, and its own condition c2c1−c0>0c_2c_1-c_0>0 again holds as a sum of positive terms.

Each window edge meets the spectral conditions of the Hopf theorem. At both edges of both windows a simple pair of eigenvalues crosses the imaginary axis at nonzero speed, near ±0.981i\pm0.981i for the annihilation controller, while the other eigenvalues stay in the left half-plane. The branch type was not computed.

The cycle at k=10k=10 attracts nearby trajectories. Its nontrivial Floquet multipliers, the factors by which a small deviation from the cycle is multiplied over one period, have moduli of at most 0.171, inside the unit circle. That is numerical evidence that the orbit is locally orbitally stable.

The experimentSigW and RsiW in E. coli

The experiment

Aoki and colleagues built the pair in Escherichia coli from the Bacillus subtilis sigma factor SigW and its anti-sigma factor RsiW, which sequesters it (p. 535). After a protease was induced, the closed loop showed virtually no change in its fluorescent reporter, while the open loop lost more than 40% in most conditions tested (p. 536).14 Their theory assumes negligible degradation of the controller proteins, which living cells do not satisfy, and their simulations with realistic parameters give small errors (p. 535). In growing cells the adaptation is near-perfect, not exact.

Two refinements stay outside the clock. Moving the actuation from the reference species to the sensor species changes the noise, not the set point of the mean (optional A3). In a noisy network the pair still adapts in the mean (optional A4).

The frequency calculation explains the local stability tradeoff. The Bode sensitivity appendix derives the controller transfer, reproduces this two-stage instability window and compares three actuation choices. It also states why dilution and windup need different conclusions.

Use the sequestering pair's identity: the difference of the controller totals integrates the error exactly at every binding allocation, so any rest has X=μ/θX=\mu/\theta and the actuator holds the compensating action. Before trusting it, check three things separately: a reachable set point, a controller leak small enough for the error you can accept, and a stable rest for the actual plant.

A15Generalize the feedforward rate laws

Return to Lecture 9's incoherent feedforward loop, in its simplest form. The input makes the output and also its degrader, and the output settles at a level with no input in it, because the input went into the degrader, in proportion. No constant had to match. What must match are reaction orders, and Lecture 9's two implementations adapted where their effective orders nearly matched.

The circuitThe input makes the output and its degrader

The simplest version has three species. The input W makes the output X1X_1 at rate k1wk_1w and its degrader X2X_2 at rate k2wk_2w, where w is W's concentration. X2X_2 removes X1X_1, a process the model does not resolve, with the rate law δx1x2\delta x_1x_2, and X2X_2 is itself removed at rate γx2\gamma x_2 (Figure 29). Lower-case letters are concentrations:

x˙1=k1w−δx1x2,x˙2=k2w−γx2.\dot x_1=k_1w-\delta x_1x_2,\qquad \dot x_2=k_2w-\gamma x_2.(E8)

The output settles at a level with no input in it. At rest x2∗=k2w/γx_2^*=k_2w/\gamma, and then

x1∗=k1wδx2∗=k1γk2δ,x_1^*=\frac{k_1w}{\delta x_2^*}=\frac{k_1\gamma}{k_2\delta},(E9)

for every constant w>0w>0. Feedforward loops are common in transcription networks, but prevalence is not function: in E. coli most of them (85%) are coherent, not incoherent.15

The memoryThe input is stored in the degrader

The input went into the degrader, in proportion. The degrader's steady level k2w/γk_2w/\gamma is proportional to the input, and it holds the input while the output returns. After a step in w the output pulses, then returns as the degrader catches up. At k1=k2=δ=γ=1k_1=k_2=\delta=\gamma=1, a tenfold step in w makes the output peak at 2.629 times its set point, 0.3733 time units after the step, and then return exactly, while the degrader rises tenfold (Figure 18, model predictions).

The mechanism or curve is shown in the main-route figure. The calculation below supplies its detailed audit.

The ordersWhat must match are reaction orders

No constant had to match, so A9's compensator failure does not apply. Change any of the four rate constants k1k_1, k2k_2, δ\delta and γ\gamma, and the output still returns to a level with no input in it. Only that level moves.

What must match are reaction orders. In this simplest example the input enters both production paths at the same order, the first. The degrader acts on the output at the order at which it is itself removed, also the first. For monomial rate laws the general condition is one product of orders (optional A5).

Adaptation fails when the orders stop matching. Saturate the degrader's removal, and x2x_2 no longer tracks the input in proportion. Add an input-independent leak k0k_0 to the output's production, and x1∗=(k1w+k0)γ/(k2δw)x_1^*=(k_1w+k_0)\gamma/(k_2\delta w) depends on w. Add a second sink for the output, −ℓx1-\ell x_1, and the output depends on w again (A16). At those constants, a tenfold input step then moves the steady output by −47.4% with a saturating removal γKx2/(K+x2)\gamma Kx_2/(K+x_2) at K=20K=20, by −30% with a leak k0=0.5k_0=0.5, and by +81.8% with a load ℓ=1\ell=1 (Figure 20, model predictions).

Lecture 9's two implementations adapted where their effective orders nearly matched. Degradation adapted only while the degrader stayed free and below KdK_d, and repression only while the repressor exceeded KdK_d and its promoter total (Lecture 9, §6). Those windows are where the effective orders approximately match, not where they are exactly equal.

The order-change comparison is shown in the main-route figure. This section derives its generalized rate-law condition.

Check an incoherent feedforward loop for exact adaptation by its reaction orders, not its constants: in the simplest loop the input must enter both paths at one order, and the degrader must act on the output at the order of its own removal. Expect a saturated removal, a leak or a second sink to break it.

A natural feedforward adapter. Is there a natural circuit that adapts perfectly by an incoherent feedforward loop, with its molecules known? Ras activation in Dictyostelium chemotaxis has been proposed. Takeda and colleagues stepped the chemoattractant cAMP and followed activated Ras through a reporter, RBD-GFP, that moves from the cytosol to the membrane, so the measured cytosolic signal falls and then returns. It returned to its prestimulus level within 35 s for steps from 10−210^{-2} to 10310^3 nM. Of the two simple topologies that can adapt perfectly, only the incoherent feedforward model fitted the data, in particular because the integral-feedback model's adaptation kinetics depended strongly on the step size, unlike the data.19 Read that result within its limits. It is a model-fitting result that compares only the tested feedback models. The roles of the activator RasGEF and the inhibitor RasGAP are inferred from the fit, and the authors keep open that adaptation happens upstream of RasGEF. Their latrunculin B test removes feedback through actin, and it is not a test of a load on the output. Which of the three experiments of A17 would settle the wiring?

A16Use an output load to distinguish adaptive mechanisms

Input cancellation can hide an error-integrating coordinate. In the incoherent feedforward loop, a combination of the output and the degrader changes at a rate proportional to the error. No molecule carries it. Test what this identity survives while holding the reference constants fixed. Input invariance, a fixed set point and robustness to a load are three different properties, and an extra sink on the output tells the two designs apart.

The coordinateAn integral that no molecule carries

Cancel the common input to find what can change only while the output is off its set point. In (E8), the input terms have coefficients k1k_1 and k2k_2. Subtract k1/k2k_1/k_2 times the degrader equation from the output equation. This motivates the coordinate z=x1−(k1/k2)x2z=x_1-(k_1/k_2)x_2, with units of concentration, and gives

z˙=δx2(x1∗−x1),\dot z=\delta x_2\big(x_1^*-x_1\big),(E10)

with x1∗x_1^* the steady output (E9). So z changes at the rate of the error, with a positive gain δx2\delta x_2 that depends on the state, and it can rest only where x1=x1∗x_1=x_1^*. After the tenfold step of Figure 18, z moves from 0 to x1∗−(k1/k2)x2∗=1−10=−9x_1^*-(k_1/k_2)x_2^*=1-10=-9 and rests there (Figure 19, model prediction).

No molecule carries z. It is a coordinate, established here directly by subtraction, so the reaction graph has no feedback edge while the dynamics contain an internal memory of the input. The loop is therefore no counterexample to the internal model principle. Nor is (E10) an application of the classical theorem of A10, whose hypotheses on the input and on robustness differ. The transformed equations fit Sontag's output-driven form, but his global hypotheses have not all been checked for this loop (optional A1).

The mechanism or curve is shown in the main-route figure. The calculation below supplies its detailed audit.

Robust to what?Three properties, with the reference fixed

Robust to what? Hold the reference constants fixed first. For the sequestering pair, μ\mu and θ\theta set the reference μ/θ\mu/\theta, so changing them changes the reference itself. Compare the designs under changes of the plant and of the load, with μ\mu and θ\theta fixed. Three properties then differ.

Input invariance: both designs have it. The incoherent feedforward loop keeps it under any positive change of its four rate constants, which is why it needs no matched constant.

A fixed set point: the pair has it, and the incoherent feedforward loop does not. The incoherent feedforward loop's set point k1γ/(k2δ)k_1\gamma/(k_2\delta) moves when those constants change, while the pair keeps μ/θ\mu/\theta when the plant's removal or actuation changes. In the model, over 20 random sets of the four constants, the feedforward output stays input invariant while its set point ranges from 0.00183 to 120. Over 20 random sets of the plant's constants, with μ\mu and θ\theta fixed, the pair rests at μ/θ\mu/\theta every time (model predictions).

Robustness to a load: the pair has it if it can recover, and the incoherent feedforward loop does not. An extra input-independent first-order sink on the output, −ℓx1-\ell x_1, gives

x1∗=k1wδk2w/γ+ℓ,x_1^*=\frac{k_1w}{\delta k_2w/\gamma+\ell},(E11)

which depends on w, so the incoherent feedforward loop stops adapting. With ℓ=1\ell=1 at the constants of Figure 18, (E11) gives 1/(1+1)=0.51/(1+1)=0.5 at w=1w=1 and 10/(10+1)=0.909110/(10+1)=0.9091 at w=10w=10, a shift of +81.8%. The pair returns to μ/θ\mu/\theta under a load on X if the set point stays reachable and the recovery is stable. In the model it returns after the load, and again after the removal of X doubles (Figure 30, model predictions).

Chemotaxis showed the same split between an adaptive property and a reference value. Its precision was robust to the protein levels, and its steady tumbling rate was not (A12).4

PropertyIncoherent feedforward loop (E8)Sequestering pair (E7), μ\mu and θ\theta fixed
Input invarianceYes, under any positive change of k1k_1, k2k_2, δ\delta and γ\gammaYes, at any rest
A fixed set pointNo: k1γ/(k2δ)k_1\gamma/(k_2\delta) moves with the constantsYes: μ/θ\mu/\theta, when the plant's removal or actuation changes
Robustness to the load −ℓx1-\ell x_1No: the output (E11) depends on wYes, if the set point stays reachable and the recovery is stable

Find an incoherent feedforward loop's integral as a coordinate, here z=x1−(k1/k2)x2z=x_1-(k_1/k_2)x_2, and reconcile adaptation without a feedback edge with the internal model principle. Before calling a design robust, name the change: input invariance, a fixed set point and a load are different tests, and a load on the output separates the incoherent feedforward loop from the pair.

A17Compare exactness, feasibility and operating range

Assess adaptation with three separate tests: an identity of the stated model, the validity of any kinetic approximation, and a reachable, stable operating range. Lecture 8's regimes organize the limiting laws, but an identity can stay exact while feasibility or stability fails. Sorting each mechanism this way names the experiment that would break it.

The sortIdentity, limiting law, operating range

Some exactness is an identity of the stated model. The sequestering pair's subtraction (E7) holds at every binding allocation. The incoherent feedforward loop's matched orders give the same steady output (E9) for every constant positive input, an identity of its rate laws (E8). At zero input the degrader decays to zero and the output stops wherever it happens to be, so that argument needs the input positive.

Some exactness is a limiting law, created by a kinetic approximation. Zero order in a saturated cycle, the joint regime of the two-cycle feedback circuit and the approximately matched effective orders of Lecture 9's binding implementations are such laws. Lecture 8's regimes organize them. Each law holds until its approximation fails: the methylation sites fill, or an enzyme leaves saturation.

A regime justifies a limiting law, and each measured quantity then has its own range. At set PT the two-cycle feedback circuit's joint regime runs from qI=0.052q_I=0.052 to 20. The partial pool A∗+C3A^*+C_3 stays within 5% of σ\sigma from 0.065 to at least 10410^4, far past the regime's upper edge. The full total stays within 5% only from 0.064 to 5.23. Each quantity's accuracy comes from the exact decomposition (E16), so leaving the regime does not by itself end the partial pool's adaptation (A13, optional A7).

Either kind needs a feasible, stable operating range. The set point must be reachable and the rest must be stable. That range is not automatically one of Lecture 8's winner regimes, and an identity can stay exact while feasibility or stability fails, as windup and the two-stage instability show.

The experimentsThree ways to tell two adaptive circuits apart

Three experiments tell two adaptive circuits with the same trace apart. Add a load to the output: the sequestering pair returns, if it can, and the incoherent feedforward loop shifts (A16). Delete or clamp the memory, as a cheR deletion does in chemotaxis: in the model, methylation drains to the floor, the activity falls to 2.5×10−32.5\times10^{-3}, and an attractant step then lowers it to 7.1×10−87.1\times10^{-8} with no return (Figure 31, left). Push the input past the adapting quantity's own 5% range: for the receptor activity in the model that range ends at L=28.1 KIL=28.1\,K_I, and after a step to 100KI100K_I the sites fill and the activity settles at 0.0039, 98.8% below a∗a^* (Figure 31, right).

Model meets measurement

Both chemotaxis experiments have been done in E. coli. A strain deleted for cheR did not tumble and could not adapt (p. 169), as the model's low activity with no return predicts.4 Precision falls at high attractant, as A12 reported from Neumann and colleagues' measurements, with the filling of the sites as their inferred cause.10

The capabilityFive questions place any adaptive circuit

Five questions place any adaptive circuit. Name its memory. Name the quantity that adapts. Say whether its exactness is an identity or a limiting law. Say what bounds it. And name the experiment that would break it. The table above answers them for the mechanisms of this lecture.

Lecture 11 makes the order statements systematic. This lecture used reaction orders by intuition: a zero-order removal makes an integrator inside an operating range, and an incoherent feedforward loop adapts when the orders of its rate laws satisfy one product condition. Each such limiting law holds only inside a regime whose edges set its range. Lecture 11 locates those regimes with reaction-order geometry. The exact identities need no regime. Their limits are reachability and stability.

Sort any adaptive circuit by its memory, the quantity that adapts, the source of its exactness (an identity or a limiting law), what bounds it, and the experiment that breaks it: add a load to the output, delete the memory, or push the input past the range.

A18Compare the discrete controller with a continuous-time construction

A discrete update and a continuous-time equation have different stability tests. The same equilibrium reasoning applies to both, but the clock and gains must be stated.

The continuous-time plant changes at the unbalanced drive. Write y˙=w−u\dot y=w-u. With z˙=y\dot z=y and u=kIzu=k_Iz, a constant disturbance gives y¨+kIy=0\ddot y+k_Iy=0. This particular integral-only construction oscillates with constant amplitude. The discrete integral-only rule of §3 also has bounded oscillations. Its new-output memory update matters. Accumulating the previous output instead adds a delay and changes the stability.

Proportional action supplies damping in the continuous-time example. Taking u=kPy+kIzu=k_Py+k_Iz gives y¨+kPy˙+kIy=0\ddot y+k_P\dot y+k_Iy=0. Positive gains make this two-state continuous loop settle. At kP=2k_P=2, kI=1k_I=1 and a unit disturbance from y=z=0y=z=0, the output is y=te−ty=t e^{-t} and the action is u=1+(t−1)e−tu=1+(t-1)e^{-t}.

State the clock, the update convention and the gains before transferring a convergence claim between discrete and continuous controllers.

A19Check which output adapts beyond the bilinear binding regime

The bilinear approximation makes free and total output nearly equal. Outside that approximation, an experiment that counts free output can give a different answer from one that counts the bound output too.

The steady balances fix how much degrader is occupied. Use the resolved mechanism of section 9, including removal of bound degrader with release of intact output. The exact total balances at constant w>0w>0 give q2∗=k2w/γq_2^*=k_2w/\gamma and C12∗=k1w/kcatC_{12}^*=k_1w/k_\mathrm{cat}. Define the occupied fraction of degrader by

r=C12∗q2∗=k1γkcatk2.r=\frac{C_{12}^*}{q_2^*}=\frac{k_1\gamma}{k_\mathrm{cat}k_2}.

The occupied fraction is independent of the input. A finite positive steady state needs 0<r<10<r<1, so some degrader remains free. The free degrader is X2∗=(1−r)q2∗X_2^*=(1-r)q_2^*. Setting the complex balance to zero gives X1∗X2∗=KMC12∗X_1^*X_2^*=K_MC_{12}^*, where KM=(k−+kcat+γ)/k+K_M=(k_-+k_\mathrm{cat}+\gamma)/k_+. Dividing the bound and free degrader amounts then gives

X1∗=KMr1−r,q1∗=X1∗+C12∗=KMr1−r+rk2wγ.X_1^*=K_M\frac{r}{1-r},\qquad q_1^*=X_1^*+C_{12}^*=K_M\frac{r}{1-r}+r\frac{k_2w}{\gamma}.

The two observables therefore answer different adaptation questions. The free output contains no input w. The total output adds the occupied complex, whose amount increases with w. This conclusion is exact at a positive steady state of the specified resolved mechanism. It is a steady-state calculation, rather than a proof of convergence from every initial state.

The bilinear limit makes the two observables nearly equal. Rapid reversible binding uses Kd=k−/k+K_d=k_-/k_+. Mostly free output and degrader require r≪1r\ll1 and k2w/γ≪Kdk_2w/\gamma\ll K_d. Then X1∗≈KdrX_1^*\approx K_dr and the bound contribution is small. The figure isolates this binding-equilibrium limit with KdK_d. For the resolved steady state, use KMK_M instead.

The capacity condition fails when all the degrader would have to be occupied. If r≥1r\ge1, no finite positive steady state can supply the required free degrader. This failure concerns feasibility. Measuring a different output cannot remove that capacity limit.

In this resolved mechanism, increasing the input can leave free output unchanged while increasing the amount bound to degrader. Test the observable actually being measured.

A20Antithetic actuation redistributes disturbance sensitivity across frequency

A3 compares controllers with the same adapting mean but different noise. A14 shows dilution, windup and instability. The Bode sensitivity integral answers a narrower question: which changes in the response to small disturbances must compensate each other across frequency?

The three actuation routes share the integral identity. Use the ideal annihilation controller Z˙1=μ−ηZ1Z2\dot Z_1=\mu-\eta Z_1Z_2 and Z˙2=θX−ηZ1Z2\dot Z_2=\theta X-\eta Z_1Z_2, with positive constants and no controller dilution. The reference produces Z1Z_1, and the output X produces the sensor Z2Z_2. Production of the controlled plant is v=h(Z1,Z2)v=h(Z_1,Z_2). Their difference obeys d(Z1−Z2)/dt=μ−θXd(Z_1-Z_2)/dt=\mu-\theta X, so every equilibrium has X∗=μ/θX^*=\mu/\theta. Moving the actuation changes how that equilibrium is reached.

Specify the disturbance before defining sensitivity

We compare an additive production disturbance at a positive equilibrium. Hold μ and θ fixed. Let δd\delta d be a small extra production rate entering the plant alongside δv\delta v, and measure the output displacement δX\delta X. A one-stage plant obeys δX˙=δv+δd−γδX\delta\dot X=\delta v+\delta d-\gamma\delta X. A two-stage plant instead obeys δM˙=δv+δd−γMδM\delta\dot M=\delta v+\delta d-\gamma_M\delta M and δX˙=βδM−γXδX\delta\dot X=\beta\delta M-\gamma_X\delta X. Their plant transfer functions are

P(s)=1s+γorP(s)=β(s+γM)(s+γX).P(s)=\frac{1}{s+\gamma}\quad\text{or}\quad P(s)=\frac{\beta}{(s+\gamma_M)(s+\gamma_X)}.

The Laplace variable s has units of inverse time. The production disturbance and actuation have the same units. All following frequency responses describe small perturbations about this equilibrium.

Moving actuation changes the proportional contribution

The controller's local response reveals the difference between the routes. Define the two annihilation frequencies A=ηZ2∗A=\eta Z_2^* and B=ηZ1∗B=\eta Z_1^*, and c=A+Bc=A+B. Linearization gives

δZ˙1=−AδZ1−BδZ2,δZ˙2=θδX−AδZ1−BδZ2.\begin{aligned} \delta\dot Z_1&=-A\delta Z_1-B\delta Z_2,\\ \delta\dot Z_2&=\theta\delta X-A\delta Z_1-B\delta Z_2. \end{aligned}

The actuation slopes select which controller species acts on production. Define g1=∂h/∂Z1≥0g_1=\partial h/\partial Z_1\ge0 and g2=−∂h/∂Z2≥0g_2=-\partial h/\partial Z_2\ge0, evaluated at the equilibrium. Then δv=g1δZ1−g2δZ2\delta v=g_1\delta Z_1-g_2\delta Z_2. Reference-only actuation has g1>0,g2=0g_1>0,g_2=0. Sensor-only actuation represses production and has g1=0,g2>0g_1=0,g_2>0. Sensor-and-reference actuation has both slopes positive.

Solving the two controller balances gives a negative-feedback transfer function. With zero initial perturbations,

δZ1(s)=−θBs(s+c)δX(s),δZ2(s)=θ(s+A)s(s+c)δX(s).\delta Z_1(s)=-\frac{\theta B}{s(s+c)}\delta X(s),\qquad \delta Z_2(s)=\frac{\theta(s+A)}{s(s+c)}\delta X(s).

Therefore δv(s)=−C(s)δX(s)\delta v(s)=-C(s)\delta X(s), where

C(s)=θ[g2s+g1B+g2A]s(s+c)=θs+c[g2+g1B+g2As].C(s)=\frac{\theta\left[g_2s+g_1B+g_2A\right]}{s(s+c)} =\frac{\theta}{s+c}\left[g_2+\frac{g_1B+g_2A}{s}\right].

Sensor-only actuation supplies a proportional contribution as well as integration. The term g2g_2 in brackets is the proportional contribution, filtered by 1/(s+c)1/(s+c). Both reference-only actuation and sensor-only actuation retain the low-frequency integral coefficient KI=θ(g1B+g2A)/cK_I=\theta(g_1B+g_2A)/c, which has units of inverse time squared. This local calculation connects the hidden proportional action discussed in A3 to the transient response. It does not establish the stochastic noise claim by itself.

The same Bode sensitivity integral permits different maximum sensitivities

Sensitivity measures disturbance attenuation relative to the uncontrolled plant. Define the loop transfer function L(s)=P(s)C(s)L(s)=P(s)C(s) and the sensitivity function S(s)=1/[1+L(s)]S(s)=1/[1+L(s)]. The production-disturbance response is δX(s)=P(s)S(s)δd(s)\delta X(s)=P(s)S(s)\delta d(s). Without control it is P(s)δd(s)P(s)\delta d(s). Thus S is the dimensionless ratio of the two responses. It is not itself their dimensional disturbance-to-output transfer function.

Integral action rejects a small constant production disturbance when the loop settles. At low frequency, C(s)∼KI/sC(s)\sim K_I/s, so S(0)=0S(0)=0 for either plant above. This is the frequency-domain version of the zero-error equilibrium condition. Internal stability must still be checked.

The Bode sensitivity integral constrains the entire stable frequency response. Let ω be angular frequency, in radians per unit time. The needed theorem is the following.

Bode sensitivity integral

For a real-rational single-input, single-output loop with an internally asymptotically stable closed loop and L(s)=O(s−2)L(s)=O(s^{-2}) as ∣s∣→∞|s|\to\infty,

∫0∞ln⁡∣S(iω)∣ dω=π∑Re⁡pj>0Re⁡pj,\int_0^\infty\ln|S(i\omega)|\,d\omega =\pi\sum_{\operatorname{Re}p_j>0}\operatorname{Re}p_j,

where the pjp_j are the right-half-plane poles of L, counted with multiplicity.

The integral is improper at zero when the controller contains an integrator. The logarithmic singularity is integrable because ln⁡∣S(iω)∣∼ln⁡ω+constant\ln|S(i\omega)|\sim\ln\omega+\text{constant}. The theorem and its high-frequency qualification are stated in Åström and Murray, Theorem 14.3 and Exercise 14.3.

All three routes have the same zero Bode sensitivity integral for the plants specified here. Their loop transfer functions have no right-half-plane poles. The controller can retain a pole at the origin. Each plant is strictly proper, and every controller above decays at least as 1/s1/s, so every loop satisfies L(s)=O(s−2)L(s)=O(s^{-2}). Whenever the closed loop is internally stable,

∫0∞ln⁡∣S(iω)∣ dω=0.\int_0^\infty\ln|S(i\omega)|\,d\omega=0.

Low-frequency attenuation must be compensated at other frequencies. Since ∣S∣<1|S|<1 near zero, ln⁡∣S∣\ln|S| is negative there. A zero integral requires a positive contribution elsewhere, where ∣S∣>1|S|>1. This redistribution is the waterbed effect. The conserved quantity is signed logarithmic area with respect to dωd\omega. It does not fix the maximum sensitivity or phase margin. Olsman and colleagues use this perspective to organize antithetic performance tradeoffs. Their model and tradeoff analysis provide the biological connection.

Compare the routes at the same equilibrium and integral gain

A fair comparison fixes the equilibrium, plant and low-frequency integral gain. Use concentration unit qrefq_\mathrm{ref} and time unit 1/γref1/\gamma_\mathrm{ref}. Set Z1∗=Z2∗=X∗=qrefZ_1^*=Z_2^*=X^*=q_\mathrm{ref}, θ=A=B=γref\theta=A=B=\gamma_\mathrm{ref}, and all plant relaxation frequencies and β equal to γref\gamma_\mathrm{ref}. Choose the slopes below. The controller constants are η=γref/qref\eta=\gamma_\mathrm{ref}/q_\mathrm{ref} and μ=qrefγref\mu=q_\mathrm{ref}\gamma_\mathrm{ref}. Every route has KI=γref2K_I=\gamma_\mathrm{ref}^2.

Here sˉ=s/γref\bar s=s/\gamma_\mathrm{ref}, Cˉ=C/γref\bar C=C/\gamma_\mathrm{ref} and Pˉ=γrefP\bar P=\gamma_\mathrm{ref}P. The numerical comparison uses Pˉ=1/(sˉ+1)\bar P=1/(\bar s+1) or 1/(sˉ+1)21/(\bar s+1)^2. It varies the actuation route without increasing the common integral coefficient.

These slopes can arise at the same positive production rate. For example, take h∗=qrefγrefh^*=q_\mathrm{ref}\gamma_\mathrm{ref} and the illustrative positive law

h(Z1,Z2)=h∗exp⁡[g1h∗(Z1−qref)−g2h∗(Z2−qref)].h(Z_1,Z_2)=h^*\exp\left[ \frac{g_1}{h^*}(Z_1-q_\mathrm{ref}) -\frac{g_2}{h^*}(Z_2-q_\mathrm{ref})\right].

Each listed pair gives the required equilibrium value and derivatives. This is a local comparison realized by declared smooth production laws. The derivative g1=2γrefg_1=2\gamma_\mathrm{ref} is not an assertion that production globally equals 2γrefZ12\gamma_\mathrm{ref}Z_1.

The maximum sensitivity and phase margin require separate calculations. Define the maximum sensitivity MS=max⁡ω≥0∣S(iω)∣M_S=\max_{\omega\ge0}|S(i\omega)|. Its reciprocal is the minimum distance of the Nyquist curve L from the critical point −1. The phase margin is the extra phase lag needed to reach −180° at a frequency where ∣L∣=1|L|=1. The gain margin below is the factor by which the entire controller gain can increase before local instability.

The ∞ entries mean that this ideal local model remains stable as the controller gain is increased. They do not guarantee tolerance to delay, neglected dynamics or actuator saturation. All six stated equilibria were checked using the full linearized controller and plant.

Sensor-only actuation improves the displayed margins without removing the integral. In this example its proportional contribution changes the maximum sensitivity and spreads the compensating response across frequency. The maximum sensitivity becomes smaller and the phase margin larger than for reference-only actuation. The Bode sensitivity integral remains zero. Integral action therefore does not, by itself, order the stability margins of different controller architectures.

Use local frequency response for stability, and the full model for windup

A14 disturbs output removal rather than production. A small change δγX\delta\gamma_X adds −X∗δγX-X^*\delta\gamma_X to the output equation. For the two-stage plant, its local transfer to the output is −X∗S(s)/(s+γX)-X^*S(s)/(s+\gamma_X). The loop transfer function L and sensitivity function S are the same as above. The disturbance enters at a different point, so the prefactor differs from P. Sensitivity still measures attenuation relative to the same uncontrolled removal disturbance.

A14's gain sweep changes the equilibrium as well as the gain. For its two-stage plant with h=kZ1h=kZ_1, η=100\eta=100 and μ=θ=β=γM=γX=1\mu=\theta=\beta=\gamma_M=\gamma_X=1 in the stated units, the equilibrium gives A=kA=k, B=100/kB=100/k and c=k+100/kc=k+100/k. The exact local loop is

L(s)=100s(s+c)(s+1)2.L(s)=\frac{100}{s(s+c)(s+1)^2}.

That loop explains the stability window in A14. Its characteristic polynomial is s4+(c+2)s3+(2c+1)s2+cs+100s^4+(c+2)s^3+(2c+1)s^2+cs+100. The Routh–Hurwitz condition reduces to 2c(c+1)2>100(c+2)22c(c+1)^2>100(c+2)^2. It holds at k=1k=1, fails at k=10k=10, and holds again at k=100k=100. The unstable interval is 2.00384<k<49.904092.00384<k<49.90409. Indeed, k = 1 and k = 100 give the same c and the same local sensitivity function. A larger actuation gain does not produce a monotone loss of margin in this chemical model.

The zero-integral theorem applies only on the stable sides of that window. At k = 10 the equilibrium is unstable, so its linear sensitivity function is not the response of a settling regulator. A14's sustained nonlinear cycle requires its trajectory and stability analysis. A Bode integral about an equilibrium cannot establish that cycle.

Dilution removes zero-frequency rejection even when the Bode sensitivity integral stays zero. If both controller species dilute at rate λ, the difference obeys z˙=μ−θX−λz\dot z=\mu-\theta X-\lambda z. At the new equilibrium, the same calculation gives

Cλ(s)=θ[g2(s+λ+A)+g1B](s+λ)(s+λ+A+B).C_\lambda(s)= \frac{\theta\left[g_2(s+\lambda+A)+g_1B\right]} {(s+\lambda)(s+\lambda+A+B)}.

For λ>0\lambda>0, Cλ(0)C_\lambda(0) is finite and generally Sλ(0)>0S_\lambda(0)>0. A persistent small disturbance can leave an offset. For an internally stable closed loop with either strictly proper plant above, the full Bode sensitivity integral is still zero. The integral constrains frequency redistribution. The origin pole determines exact rejection of a constant disturbance.

Windup is a failure of reachability. If the required output lies beyond the actuator ceiling, there is no operating equilibrium at that target. The error integral keeps accumulating. The local sensitivity integral cannot replace A14's finite-amplitude calculation or its inventory and actuation bounds.

Intrinsic chemical noise requires all reaction-noise channels. A stationary output variance depends on their strengths, correlations and transfers through the linearized network. The function S above treats one externally imposed disturbance. It cannot alone prove the noise comparison in A3, or replace that section's stochastic assumptions. The additional proportional contribution explains one dynamical difference between the architectures. Their molecular noise still needs its own calculation.

The high-frequency plant model determines whether the integrals remain equal. The equality above uses a strictly proper plant. If a model instead treats the plant as an instantaneous gain P0>0P_0>0, sensor-only actuation and sensor-and-reference actuation give lim⁡s→∞sL(s)=P0θg2\lim_{s\to\infty}sL(s)=P_0\theta g_2. The generalized formula then gives an integral −πP0θg2/2-\pi P_0\theta g_2/2, while reference-only actuation still gives zero. An instantaneous approximation changes the high-frequency hypothesis. To apply the zero-integral result to a cell, retain the plant dynamics over the frequencies that contribute. Åström and Murray, Exercise 14.3.

The three actuation routes share the same Bode sensitivity integral for the stated dynamic plants. They can have different maximum sensitivities, stability margins and intrinsic noise. Check the disturbance, equilibrium, high-frequency dynamics and stability before interpreting the conserved logarithmic area.

Teaching route

Choose optional branches around the explanatory sequence

The explanation determines the length. The main route develops the function, tries controllers, implements memory chemically, and reopens the feedforward question. Optional branches answer further questions at the points where they arise.

Teaching taskSupporting branch
Discover a controller through its updates (§§2–3)State-model memory bookkeeping (A8), the older linear comparison (A9), and continuous-time dynamics (A18)
Implement integral memory with chemistry (§§4–7)The main three-construction comparison (§3b), detailed chemotaxis assumptions (A12), and measured pools (A7,A13)
Compare exact stoichiometry with limiting kinetics (§8)Stochastic scope (A4), actuator limits and plant stability (A14)
Explain the feedforward reversal (§§9–11)General reaction orders (A5,A15), fold-change detection (A6), output loads (A16), and the operating-range audit (A17)
Ask when a regulator must contain an integralThe main internal model statement (§3a), with nonlinear hypotheses in A1 and A10

Choose optional material by the question the audience needs answered. The exact-balance-to-regime calculation and the response that it predicts belong together. A detailed theorem, parameter sweep or alternative experimental test can be taken when its question arises.

Questions to develop further

  1. Choose another cellular function. Specify its input, output, performance and physical implementation.
  2. For one adaptive mechanism, locate a regime boundary and predict which observable will stop adapting first.
  3. Compare two circuits with the same adaptive trace under an output load, dilution or a change in enzyme abundance.

All numerical figures and every number marked as a model prediction come from model calculations at illustrative parameters, read from the saved data of the Lecture 10 analysis or from Lecture 9's verified curves. They are not fits to data. Figure generators, the data they read and the numbered checks are kept in the Lecture 10 research directory.
